notes.Article:
## Overview
An article is written for a school magazine, a newsletter or a website. Your reader is usually other students. You give information and your opinions in an interesting, lively way.
- From 2024: 120–160 words, 15 marks (6 for content, 9 for language).
- Older papers: 100–150 words, 12 marks (6 + 6).
## Step-by-step method
1. Underline the topic, the reader (who reads it) and where it will be published.
2. Read the comments in the speech bubbles. They are ideas you may use, but add ideas of your own.
3. Plan 4 short paragraphs: introduction, two main points, conclusion.
4. Write a catchy title.
5. Open with a question or a surprising fact to hook the reader.
6. Give each main point a reason and an example.
7. End with your opinion or a message for the reader.
8. Check your word count, spelling and linking words.
## Key ideas
### Format
- A title is expected. It can be a question: "Should we all learn to cook?"
- No greeting (no "Dear …") and no sign-off.
- Paragraphs, each with one main idea.
### Style
- Semi-formal and friendly. You may speak directly to the reader ("Have you ever …?").
- Use a range of vocabulary and sentence types.
- Show your opinion clearly: "In my view…", "I strongly believe…".
## Useful phrases
- Opening: "Have you ever wondered…?", "Imagine a school where…"
- Adding: "What is more…", "Another reason is that…"
- Contrast: "However…", "On the other hand…"
- Ending: "So, next time you…", "All in all, I think…"
## Model opening
**Task:** An article for your school magazine about whether students should do volunteer work.
"Giving a Little, Gaining a Lot. Have you ever spent a Saturday helping someone you didn't know? Last month I joined a beach clean-up, and it changed the way I see my free time…"
## More detail
### Useful phrases
- Hook: "Have you ever wondered…?" / "Imagine waking up to…"
- Giving opinion: "In my view…" / "There is no doubt that…"
- Adding: "What is more…" / "On top of that…"
- Ending: "So, why not give it a try?" / "It's time we all…"
### Model opening
**Title: Why every student should learn to swim**
"Living on an island, we are surrounded by water every single day. Yet many young people never learn to swim properly. Here's why that needs to change."
### Checklist
- Catchy title, engaging opening, clear paragraphs, direct address to readers ("you"), strong ending.
## Common mistakes
- Writing it like a letter (Dear… / Yours…).
- Copying the speech-bubble comments word for word.
- No clear opinion at the end.
## Exam tips
- Use the bubbles as a starting point, then add at least one idea of your own.
- Keep within the word limit; extra words do not earn extra marks.
notes.Essay:
## Overview
An essay is written for your teacher. It discusses a statement or question in a balanced, formal way and ends with your own view.
- From 2024: 120–160 words, 15 marks (6 for content, 9 for language).
- Older papers: 100–150 words, 12 marks (6 + 6).
## Step-by-step method
1. Read the statement. Decide: do you agree, disagree or partly agree?
2. Note two points for and two points against (the bubbles can help).
3. Plan: introduction, points for, points against, conclusion.
4. Introduction: restate the topic in your own words.
5. Body: give each point a reason or example.
6. Conclusion: give your opinion clearly and say why.
## Key ideas
### Format
- A title is optional. No greeting and no sign-off.
- Four short paragraphs work well.
### Style
- Formal: no slang and no short forms such as "don't" or "can't".
- Use impersonal phrases: "Many people believe…", "It could be argued that…".
- Balance first, then your view.
## Useful phrases
- "Some people argue that…", "Supporters of this idea claim…"
- "On the other hand…", "Critics point out that…"
- "In conclusion, I believe… because…"
## Model opening
**Task:** "Young people spend too much time on their phones." Write an essay giving your views.
"Mobile phones are now part of almost every teenager's day. While some people believe we use them too much, others argue that phones help us learn and keep in touch…"
## More detail
### Useful phrases
- Introducing a view: "Some people argue that…" / "It is often said that…"
- Contrasting: "However…" / "On the other hand…" / "Despite this…"
- Giving examples: "For instance…" / "A good example of this is…"
- Concluding: "To sum up…" / "Overall, I believe…"
### Model paragraph
"Firstly, social media helps teenagers stay connected with friends and family who live on other islands. For example, students who study in Malé can talk to their parents every day. However, spending hours online can affect sleep and schoolwork."
### Checklist
- Clear opinion, one main idea per paragraph, examples, balanced view, conclusion that answers the question.
## Common mistakes
- Giving only one side and no balance.
- Forgetting your own opinion at the end.
- Writing in a chatty, informal tone.
## Exam tips
- A clear structure earns language marks: use paragraphs and linking words.
- Your opinion in the conclusion must match what you wrote in the body.
notes.Report:
## Overview
A report is written for a head teacher, a manager or a club leader. It describes something that happened or something that exists, and ends with suggestions or recommendations.
- From 2024: 120–160 words, 15 marks (6 for content, 9 for language).
- Older papers: 100–150 words, 12 marks (6 + 6).
## Step-by-step method
1. Find the two jobs in the task, for example "say what was good" AND "suggest how it could be improved". You must do both.
2. Give the report a title.
3. Use short headings, for example: Introduction, What went well, Problems, Recommendations.
4. Introduction: say the purpose of the report.
5. Give facts and examples under each heading.
6. Finish with clear recommendations.
## Key ideas
### Format
- Title and headings help the reader. No greeting and no sign-off.
- Short, clear paragraphs.
### Style
- Formal and objective: report facts, not feelings.
- Passive forms are useful: "It was found that…", "It is recommended that…".
## Useful phrases
- "The aim of this report is to…"
- "Most students said that…", "A few people felt that…"
- "I would recommend that…", "It would be a good idea to…"
## Model opening
**Task:** A report for your head teacher about a school trip to a museum.
"Report on the Museum Trip. Introduction: The purpose of this report is to describe our Grade 10 visit to the National Museum and suggest how future trips could be improved…"
## More detail
### Useful phrases
- Purpose: "The aim of this report is to…"
- Findings: "Most students said…" / "It was found that…" / "According to the survey…"
- Recommending: "I would recommend that…" / "It would be a good idea to…"
### Model section
**Recommendations**
"I would recommend that the canteen offers more healthy options, such as fruit and salads, because many students said they would choose these if they were available."
### Checklist
- Title and short headings, formal language, facts before opinions, clear recommendations with reasons.
## Common mistakes
- Doing only one of the two jobs in the task.
- Writing it as a story or a letter.
- No recommendations at the end.
## Exam tips
- Headings make your organisation clear and quick to mark.
- Keep the tone polite and formal for the head teacher.
notes.Review:
## Overview
A review describes something you have tried and gives your opinion of it. It ends with a recommendation. Reviews are usually for a school magazine or a website.
- From 2024: 120–160 words, 15 marks (6 for content, 9 for language).
- Older papers: 100–150 words, 12 marks (6 + 6).
## Step-by-step method
1. Say what you are reviewing and where or when you tried it.
2. Describe it briefly: what it is and what it offers.
3. Give the good points with examples.
4. Give one or two weaker points.
5. Recommend it or not, and say who would enjoy it.
## Types of review
### Place (café, restaurant, hotel, sports centre, museum)
- Location, atmosphere, service, prices, food or facilities.
- "The staff were friendly, but the queue was rather long."
### Film or television show
- Type of film, story (no spoilers), actors, music, special effects.
- "The acting was convincing, although the ending felt rushed."
### Book
- Type of book, main characters, plot (no ending), writing style.
- "The characters are so real that I could not put it down."
### Product or app/website
- What it does, how easy it is to use, value for money, problems.
- "The app is simple to use, but it needs better offline features."
### Event (festival, concert, sports day, exhibition)
- What happened, organisation, atmosphere, highlights.
- "The highlight was the student band, who had everyone dancing."
### Coursebook, magazine or other
- Content, design, how useful it is, what could be better.
## Useful phrases
- "If you are looking for…, this is the place for you."
- "The best thing about it is…", "The only disappointment was…"
- "I would definitely recommend it to…", "It is worth a visit."
## More detail
### Useful phrases
- Describing: "set in…" / "located just a short boat ride from…"
- Praising: "a must-see" / "highly recommended" / "outstanding value"
- Criticising: "a little disappointing" / "the only drawback was…"
- Recommending: "I would recommend it to anyone who…" / "Give it a miss if…"
### Model ending
"Overall, the café is a perfect spot for students on a budget. The service could be quicker, but the food more than makes up for it. Four stars from me!"
### Checklist
- Name and introduce what you are reviewing, describe the best features, mention a weakness, give a clear recommendation and who it suits.
## Common mistakes
- Only describing, with no opinion.
- Telling the whole story of a film or book.
- No recommendation at the end.
## Exam tips
- Use descriptive adjectives: delicious, crowded, gripping, user-friendly.
- Balance good and bad points, then give a clear recommendation.
notes.Comprehension:
## Overview
You read one text (often an article or leaflet) and answer short questions. Most answers are single words or short phrases. Marks are for finding the exact detail.
## Step-by-step method
1. Read the title and the questions first, so you know what to look for.
2. Skim the whole text once for the main idea.
3. Underline key words in each question (when, why, which two…).
4. Scan the text for those key words or their synonyms. Questions follow the order of the text.
5. Write only the information asked. Keep it short.
6. If the question says "two", give exactly two separate points.
7. Check spelling of words you copy from the text.
## Key ideas
### Question words
- When → a time or date. Where → a place. Why → a reason. How → a method or way.
### Copying vs own words
- You may lift words from the text, but do not copy whole paragraphs. Extra wrong information can lose the mark.
## Worked example
**Text:** "The club, which began in 2015, now meets every Tuesday in the school library."
**Q: Where does the club meet?**
**Answer:** in the school library
**Why it scores well:**
- It gives only the place.
- It does not add the day, which was not asked.
## More detail
### Question types and how to answer
| Question asks | What to do |
|---|---|
| "Give two reasons…" | Two separate points, one per line |
| "Which phrase tells us…?" | Copy the exact short phrase from the text |
| "Explain in your own words…" | Rephrase; do not lift whole sentences |
| "What does the writer mean by…?" | Give the meaning in context |
| "Why…?" | Find the cause or purpose in the text |
### Strategy
1. Read the questions first so you know what to look for.
2. Skim the text for the general idea, then scan for key words.
3. Questions usually follow the order of the text.
4. Check the marks: 1 mark = 1 point.
### Common traps
- Writing an answer that is true in general but not stated in the text.
- Giving too much: an extra wrong detail can lose the mark.
- Mixing up the writer's opinion with facts.
## Common mistakes
- Writing long sentences that include wrong details.
- Giving one answer when the question asks for two.
- Answering from your own knowledge, not from the text.
## Easy tips
- Answers follow the order of the text.
- Look for synonyms: "started" in the question may be "began" in the text.
- Never leave a blank; a short guess may score.
notes.Multiple matching:
## Overview
You read several short texts (for example, four people talking about a hobby) and match statements to the correct person. Many statements use different words from the text.
## Step-by-step method
1. Read all the statements first and underline the key idea in each.
2. Read text A carefully and note what the person really says.
3. Go through each statement and decide if it matches text A exactly.
4. Repeat for each text.
5. Watch for "distractors": a text mentions the same topic but says something different.
6. Fill in every answer, even if unsure.
## Key ideas
### Paraphrase
- "I never had time for it before" may match "a lack of time stopped them earlier".
### Careful reading
- "I'd like to try" (future wish) is not the same as "I have tried" (past).
## Worked example
**Statement:** Which person was surprised by how difficult the activity was?
**Text B:** "I thought it would be easy, but it took me months to learn."
**Answer:** B
**Why it scores well:**
- "thought it would be easy… took months" means it was harder than expected.
## More detail
- You match statements to several short texts (for example four people's opinions).
### Method
1. Read all the statements first and underline key ideas.
2. Read each text carefully; note the main idea in the margin.
3. Look for **synonyms and paraphrases**, not the same words. ("I was nervous at first" = "felt anxious at the start".)
4. Watch for distractors: a text may mention the topic but say the opposite.
5. Do the easy matches first, then return to the harder ones.
### Useful paraphrase patterns
- "It didn't live up to my expectations" = disappointed.
- "I would do it again" = would recommend / repeat.
- "It was worth every penny" = good value.
## Common mistakes
- Matching on one shared word instead of the meaning.
- Spending too long on one statement.
## Easy tips
- Mark the line in the text that proves your answer.
- Each statement usually has only one correct person; check the instructions.
notes.Note-making:
## Overview
You read a text and complete notes under given headings. Answers must be short notes, not full sentences.
## Step-by-step method
1. Read the headings so you know what information to find.
2. Read the text and highlight points that fit each heading.
3. Check the number of bullet points under each heading.
4. Write each note in 1–5 words.
5. Make each note a different idea; do not repeat.
6. Check that each note fits its heading exactly.
## Key ideas
### Good notes
- Short, clear, from the text: "reduces stress", "costs less than gyms".
### Headings
- "Advantages" needs only good points. "Problems" needs only difficulties.
## Worked example
**Heading:** Benefits of cycling to school
**Text:** "Cycling keeps you fit, it is cheaper than taking the bus, and it causes no pollution."
**Answer:**
- keeps you fit
- cheaper than the bus
- no pollution
**Why it scores well:**
- Three separate points, each short and under the right heading.
## More detail
- You complete notes under headings using information from a text.
- Answers should be **short** (a few words), not full sentences.
- Each point must be different and must fit the heading.
### Method
1. Read the headings first and predict what kind of information you need.
2. Highlight relevant points in the text.
3. Keep the points brief but clear: "save money on transport" not "money".
4. Do not repeat the same idea under two headings.
### Example
**Heading: Benefits of learning to swim**
- improves fitness
- safety near water
- confidence
## Common mistakes
- Writing full sentences.
- Putting one idea in two bullets.
- Using information from the wrong part of the text.
## Easy tips
- Use the text's words; you do not need your own words.
- One idea per bullet point.
notes.Multiple choice (MCQ):
## Overview
You read a longer text (often an interview or article) and choose the correct answer A, B, C or D. It tests detail, opinion and the writer's purpose.
## Step-by-step method
1. Read the question stem only (not the options) and underline key words.
2. Find the part of the text that answers it.
3. Answer in your own mind first.
4. Read all four options and choose the one that matches your answer.
5. Check why each other option is wrong.
6. Never leave a question blank.
## Key ideas
### Distractors
- Wrong options often use words from the text but change the meaning.
### Gist and attitude
- "What is the writer's main purpose?" needs the whole paragraph, not one line.
## Worked example
**Text:** "At first I hated the long hours, but now I can't imagine doing anything else."
**Q: How does she feel about her job now? A bored B unsure C happy with it D tired**
**Answer:** C
**Why it scores well:**
- "can't imagine doing anything else" shows she likes it now; "hated" was only at first.
## More detail
- Read the question stem carefully before the options.
- Find the part of the text that answers it; then choose the option that matches its meaning.
- Eliminate options that are: not in the text, too extreme ("always", "never"), or true but not the answer to the question.
- Questions about the writer's purpose: inform, persuade, entertain, advise, describe.
- Questions about tone: positive, critical, humorous, nostalgic, enthusiastic.
- Never leave an answer blank; there is no penalty for guessing.
## Common mistakes
- Picking an option because it uses the same word as the text.
## Easy tips
- Look out for words like "at first", "now", "however", "but".
notes.Informal email:
## Overview
You write an email to a friend or family member (about 120–160 words) using three given prompts. Marks are for content and for language.
## Step-by-step method
1. Read the task and underline the three prompts.
2. Plan one short paragraph for each prompt, adding a detail or reason to each.
3. Start with a friendly greeting: "Hi Sara,".
4. Open with one or two friendly sentences.
5. Write the three paragraphs using linking words.
6. Close in a friendly way and sign off: "Write back soon, Ali".
7. Check the word count, spelling and tenses.
## Key ideas
### Informal language
- Contractions (I'm, can't), friendly questions, phrasal verbs.
### Useful phrases
- "Guess what!", "I can't wait to…", "By the way…", "Anyway, that's all for now."
## Worked example
**Task:** Email a friend about a school trip: where you went, what you enjoyed, what you will do next time.
**Model answer (start):** Hi Hana, Guess what! Last week our class went on a snorkelling trip to a nearby island. The water was so clear that we saw turtles and colourful fish. My favourite part was…
**Why it scores well:**
- Friendly tone and opening.
- Covers prompt one with details.
## More detail
### Layout
- Greeting: "Hi Aisha," or "Dear Ahmed,"
- Opening paragraph: friendly reply or reason for writing.
- Body paragraphs: one for each bullet point in the task.
- Closing: "Write back soon," / "Best wishes," + your first name.
### Language
- Contractions (I'm, can't), friendly questions ("Can you believe it?"), phrasal verbs (catch up, look forward to).
- Use descriptive detail and feelings to make it lively.
- Keep the tone right for the reader (a friend, a cousin, a teacher you know well).
### Useful phrases
- "It was great to hear from you."
- "Guess what happened last weekend?"
- "I can't wait to see you."
- "Let me know what you think."
### Marks
- Content: all three bullet points, developed with detail. Language: range of vocabulary, accurate grammar, linked paragraphs.
## Common mistakes
- Missing one of the three prompts.
- Using formal language ("Dear Sir").
- Going far over or under the word count.
## Easy tips
- One paragraph for each prompt.
- Add a reason or a feeling to every point.
notes.Listening:
## Overview
You hear recordings twice and answer short-answer, note-completion, matching and multiple-choice questions.
## Step-by-step method
1. Use the reading time to read every question and underline key words.
2. Predict the type of answer (number, place, name, reason).
3. On the first listening, write quick answers.
4. On the second listening, check and complete.
5. Spell answers correctly; numbers can be written as digits.
6. Answer every question.
## Key ideas
### Distractors
- Speakers often say one answer, then correct it: "on Monday… no, sorry, Tuesday".
### Signposts
- "The main reason is…", "Finally…", "However…".
## Worked example
**You hear:** "The museum used to open at nine, but now it opens at half past nine."
**Q: What time does the museum open now?**
**Answer:** 9:30
**Why it scores well:**
- It notices the change "now".
## More detail
- Read the questions before the audio starts; predict the type of answer (a number, a name, a place).
- Listen for signpost words: "but", "actually", "in fact" — the answer often follows them.
- Spell common words correctly; numbers and dates must be exact.
- On the second listening, check answers and fill gaps.
## Common mistakes
- Writing the first number heard.
- Writing too much and missing the next answer.
## Easy tips
- Write short answers; tidy them after the second listening.
notes.Grammar & vocabulary:
## Overview
Accurate grammar and good vocabulary raise your language marks in writing. This topic covers the most common errors.
## Key ideas
### Tenses
- Present simple for habits; present continuous for now; past simple for finished actions; present perfect for experience ("I have visited…").
### Agreement
- He/She/It + verb-s: "She lives…". Everyone/each + singular verb.
### Articles and prepositions
- a/an for one of many; the for a specific one. "interested in", "good at", "depend on".
### Vocabulary
- Replace "good, nice, bad" with precise words: delicious, exciting, disappointing.
## Step-by-step method
1. After writing, read once for tenses.
2. Read again for subject–verb agreement.
3. Check articles, plurals and prepositions.
4. Replace three simple words with better ones.
## Worked example
**Correct the sentence:** "Yesterday I go to the beach and see a turtles."
**Answer:** Yesterday I went to the beach and saw a turtle.
**Why it scores well:**
- Past tense for a finished action; "a" with a singular noun.
## More detail
### Common errors to avoid
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| He don't like it | He doesn't like it |
| I am agree | I agree |
| more better | better |
| informations, advices | information, advice |
| I have went | I have gone |
| Despite of the rain | Despite the rain |
### Tenses
- Present simple (habits), present continuous (now), past simple (finished time), present perfect (experience, unfinished time), past continuous (background), future with "will" and "going to".
### Linking words
- Addition: moreover, furthermore, in addition. Contrast: however, although, whereas. Cause: because, since, as a result, therefore. Sequence: firstly, then, finally.
### Vocabulary range
- Replace overused words: good → excellent, impressive; bad → disappointing, poor; big → enormous, huge; nice → pleasant, charming.
## Common mistakes
- Mixing tenses in one story.
- "He don't" instead of "He doesn't".
## Easy tips
- Keep a list of your own common mistakes and check for them every time.

Comprehension.front: How long should comprehension answers be?
Comprehension.back: Short: a word or a short phrase. Full sentences are not needed.

Comprehension.front: Where in the text are the answers?
Comprehension.back: In order: question 1 is near the start, the last question near the end.

Comprehension.front: What should you do before reading the text?
Comprehension.back: Read the questions first and underline the key words.

Comprehension.front: A question asks for two details. How many marks?
Comprehension.back: Usually 2 marks: one for each detail. Give exactly two.

Comprehension.front: Should you copy long chunks from the text?
Comprehension.back: No. Lift only the words that answer the question.

Comprehension.front: What do you do if a question says 'Give two reasons'?
Comprehension.back: Write two different reasons from the text, each on its own line.

Comprehension.front: How should you check spelling in your answers?
Comprehension.back: Copy names and key words carefully from the text.

Comprehension.front: What if you cannot find an answer?
Comprehension.back: Move on, then come back. Never leave a blank: make a sensible guess.

Multiple matching.front: What do you read first in multiple matching?
Multiple matching.back: The questions (statements). Then scan the texts for the same ideas.

Multiple matching.front: Will the words in the question match the text exactly?
Multiple matching.back: No. The text usually says the same idea in different words (paraphrase).

Multiple matching.front: Can one text be the answer to more than one question?
Multiple matching.back: Yes. Some texts are used more than once.

Multiple matching.front: How do you show your answer?
Multiple matching.back: Write the letter of the text (A, B, C…) on the line.
A text mentions the same topic but says something different. Check the exact meaning.

Multiple matching.front: How many questions are there in this exercise?

Multiple matching.back: Underline key words, find the matching idea, check the other texts do not match better.

Note-making.front: How long should each note be?
Note-making.back: A few words. Short notes, not full sentences.

Note-making.front: Where do the notes come from?
Note-making.back: From the text, under the headings given in the question.
Fit the heading it is under. A correct fact under the wrong heading gets no mark.

Note-making.front: Should two notes say the same thing?
Note-making.back: No. Each note must be a different point.

Note-making.front: How many points do you write?
Note-making.back: The number of lines or bullet points given under each heading.

Note-making.front: Example of a good note for 'Benefits of cycling'
Should you add your own ideas?
Note-making.back: No. Only information from the text.

Multiple choice (MCQ).front: How many options are there in each MCQ?
Multiple choice (MCQ).back: Usually three: A, B or C (check the instructions).
Read the question, find the part of the text, then choose the option with the same meaning.
They use words from the text but say something different.
Details, the writer's opinion or attitude, and the meaning of words or phrases.

Multiple choice (MCQ).front: Should you leave a question blank?
Multiple choice (MCQ).back: Never. If unsure, remove the clearly wrong options and choose.

Multiple choice (MCQ).front: How do you answer the 'writer's purpose' type?
Multiple choice (MCQ).back: Ask why the writer wrote that part: to explain, persuade, describe or warn.

Informal email.front: Who is the reader of an informal email?
Informal email.back: A friend or family member, so the tone is friendly and relaxed.

Informal email.front: How many bullet points must you cover?
Informal email.back: All three, each developed with detail. Missing one limits your content mark.

Informal email.front: How do you start an informal email?
Informal email.back: Hi / Dear + first name, then a friendly opening line, e.g. 'It was great to hear from you!'

Informal email.front: How do you end an informal email?
Informal email.back: A friendly close, e.g. 'Write back soon,' or 'Best wishes,' + your name.

Informal email.front: Name three informal features you can use
Informal email.back: Short forms (I'm), phrasal verbs (find out), friendly questions (How are you?).

Informal email.front: Should you use paragraphs in an email?
Informal email.back: Yes. One paragraph for each bullet point, plus opening and closing lines.

Article.back: Readers of a school magazine, newsletter or website, usually other students.

Article.front: Does an article need a title?

Article.back: No. No greeting and no sign-off.

Article.front: Good ways to open an article
Article.back: A question to the reader, a surprising fact, or a short story.

Article.front: What is the style of an article?
Article.back: Semi-formal and lively. You may speak directly to the reader.
With your opinion or a message for the reader.

Article.front: How do you use the comments in the bubbles?
Article.back: Use them as ideas, in your own words, and add at least one idea of your own.

Essay.front: Who is the reader of an essay?
What is the style of an essay?
Essay.back: Formal: no slang and no short forms like don't or can't.
Introduction, points for, points against, conclusion with your view.

Essay.front: Where do you give your own opinion?
Essay.back: Clearly in the conclusion (you may also show it in the introduction).

Essay.front: Phrase to present the other side
Essay.back: On the other hand… / Critics argue that…

Essay.front: What loses content marks in an essay?
Essay.back: Only one side, no examples, or no clear opinion.

Essay.front: Should an essay have a greeting?

Report.back: A head teacher, manager or club leader.

Report.back: A title, short headings and recommendations at the end.

## Overview
You read one text (often an article or leaflet) and answer short questions. Most answers are single words or short phrases. Marks are for finding the exact detail.
## Step-by-step method
1. Read the title and the questions first, so you know what to look for.
2. Skim the whole text once for the main idea.
3. Underline key words in each question (when, why, which two…).
4. Scan the text for those key words or their synonyms. Questions follow the order of the text.
5. Write only the information asked. Keep it short.
6. If the question says "two", give exactly two separate points.
7. Check spelling of words you copy from the text.
## Key ideas
### Question words
- When → a time or date. Where → a place. Why → a reason. How → a method or way.
### Copying vs own words
- You may lift words from the text, but do not copy whole paragraphs. Extra wrong information can lose the mark.
## Worked example
**Text:** "The club, which began in 2015, now meets every Tuesday in the school library."
**Q: Where does the club meet?**
**Answer:** in the school library
**Why it scores well:**
- It gives only the place.
- It does not add the day, which was not asked.
## More detail
### Question types and how to answer
| Question asks | What to do |
|---|---|
| "Give two reasons…" | Two separate points, one per line |
| "Which phrase tells us…?" | Copy the exact short phrase from the text |
| "Explain in your own words…" | Rephrase; do not lift whole sentences |
| "What does the writer mean by…?" | Give the meaning in context |
| "Why…?" | Find the cause or purpose in the text |
### Strategy
1. Read the questions first so you know what to look for.
2. Skim the text for the general idea, then scan for key words.
3. Questions usually follow the order of the text.
4. Check the marks: 1 mark = 1 point.
### Common traps
- Writing an answer that is true in general but not stated in the text.
- Giving too much: an extra wrong detail can lose the mark.
- Mixing up the writer's opinion with facts.
## Common mistakes
- Writing long sentences that include wrong details.
- Giving one answer when the question asks for two.
- Answering from your own knowledge, not from the text.
## Easy tips
- Answers follow the order of the text.
- Look for synonyms: "started" in the question may be "began" in the text.
- Never leave a blank; a short guess may score.

## Overview
You read several short texts (for example, four people talking about a hobby) and match statements to the correct person. Many statements use different words from the text.
## Step-by-step method
1. Read all the statements first and underline the key idea in each.
2. Read text A carefully and note what the person really says.
3. Go through each statement and decide if it matches text A exactly.
4. Repeat for each text.
5. Watch for "distractors": a text mentions the same topic but says something different.
6. Fill in every answer, even if unsure.
## Key ideas
### Paraphrase
- "I never had time for it before" may match "a lack of time stopped them earlier".
### Careful reading
- "I'd like to try" (future wish) is not the same as "I have tried" (past).
## Worked example
**Statement:** Which person was surprised by how difficult the activity was?
**Text B:** "I thought it would be easy, but it took me months to learn."
**Answer:** B
**Why it scores well:**
- "thought it would be easy… took months" means it was harder than expected.
## More detail
- You match statements to several short texts (for example four people's opinions).
### Method
1. Read all the statements first and underline key ideas.
2. Read each text carefully; note the main idea in the margin.
3. Look for **synonyms and paraphrases**, not the same words. ("I was nervous at first" = "felt anxious at the start".)
4. Watch for distractors: a text may mention the topic but say the opposite.
5. Do the easy matches first, then return to the harder ones.
### Useful paraphrase patterns
- "It didn't live up to my expectations" = disappointed.
- "I would do it again" = would recommend / repeat.
- "It was worth every penny" = good value.
## Common mistakes
- Matching on one shared word instead of the meaning.
- Spending too long on one statement.
## Easy tips
- Mark the line in the text that proves your answer.
- Each statement usually has only one correct person; check the instructions.

## Overview
You read a text and complete notes under given headings. Answers must be short notes, not full sentences.
## Step-by-step method
1. Read the headings so you know what information to find.
2. Read the text and highlight points that fit each heading.
3. Check the number of bullet points under each heading.
4. Write each note in 1–5 words.
5. Make each note a different idea; do not repeat.
6. Check that each note fits its heading exactly.
## Key ideas
### Good notes
- Short, clear, from the text: "reduces stress", "costs less than gyms".
### Headings
- "Advantages" needs only good points. "Problems" needs only difficulties.
## Worked example
**Heading:** Benefits of cycling to school
**Text:** "Cycling keeps you fit, it is cheaper than taking the bus, and it causes no pollution."
**Answer:**
- keeps you fit
- cheaper than the bus
- no pollution
**Why it scores well:**
- Three separate points, each short and under the right heading.
## More detail
- You complete notes under headings using information from a text.
- Answers should be **short** (a few words), not full sentences.
- Each point must be different and must fit the heading.
### Method
1. Read the headings first and predict what kind of information you need.
2. Highlight relevant points in the text.
3. Keep the points brief but clear: "save money on transport" not "money".
4. Do not repeat the same idea under two headings.
### Example
**Heading: Benefits of learning to swim**
- improves fitness
- safety near water
- confidence
## Common mistakes
- Writing full sentences.
- Putting one idea in two bullets.
- Using information from the wrong part of the text.
## Easy tips
- Use the text's words; you do not need your own words.
- One idea per bullet point.

## Overview
In Exercise 4 you read a text and write a summary of about 80–100 words (older papers: up to 80 words). You must find the right points and write them in your own words.
## Step-by-step method
1. Read the question and underline exactly what the summary is about (e.g. "the benefits of …").
2. Read the text and highlight only the points that answer the question.
3. Write each point as a short note in your own words.
4. Join the points into one paragraph using linking words (also, in addition, however, as a result).
5. Do not add your own opinions or examples.
6. Count your words and check spelling.
## Key ideas
### Content marks
- Each relevant point gets credit. Points that do not answer the question get nothing.
### Language marks
- Use your own words, not long copied phrases.
- Organise the points clearly and link them well.
## Worked example
**Summarise the advantages of cycling to school.**
Cycling is cheaper than travelling by car or bus, and it keeps students fit. In addition, it reduces traffic near the school and produces no pollution. As a result, cyclists often arrive more alert and ready to learn.
**Why it scores well:**
- Only points from the text that answer the question.
- Own words and clear linking.
## Common mistakes
- Copying whole sentences from the text.
- Adding an introduction or a conclusion with no points.
- Going far over the word limit.
## Easy tips
- Aim for 6–8 points.
- Plan with notes before you write.

## Overview
You read a longer text (often an interview or article) and choose the correct answer A, B, C or D. It tests detail, opinion and the writer's purpose.
## Step-by-step method
1. Read the question stem only (not the options) and underline key words.
2. Find the part of the text that answers it.
3. Answer in your own mind first.
4. Read all four options and choose the one that matches your answer.
5. Check why each other option is wrong.
6. Never leave a question blank.
## Key ideas
### Distractors
- Wrong options often use words from the text but change the meaning.
### Gist and attitude
- "What is the writer's main purpose?" needs the whole paragraph, not one line.
## Worked example
**Text:** "At first I hated the long hours, but now I can't imagine doing anything else."
**Q: How does she feel about her job now? A bored B unsure C happy with it D tired**
**Answer:** C
**Why it scores well:**
- "can't imagine doing anything else" shows she likes it now; "hated" was only at first.
## More detail
- Read the question stem carefully before the options.
- Find the part of the text that answers it; then choose the option that matches its meaning.
- Eliminate options that are: not in the text, too extreme ("always", "never"), or true but not the answer to the question.
- Questions about the writer's purpose: inform, persuade, entertain, advise, describe.
- Questions about tone: positive, critical, humorous, nostalgic, enthusiastic.
- Never leave an answer blank; there is no penalty for guessing.
## Common mistakes
- Picking an option because it uses the same word as the text.
## Easy tips
- Look out for words like "at first", "now", "however", "but".

## Overview
You write an email to a friend or family member (about 120–160 words) using three given prompts. Marks are for content and for language.
## Step-by-step method
1. Read the task and underline the three prompts.
2. Plan one short paragraph for each prompt, adding a detail or reason to each.
3. Start with a friendly greeting: "Hi Sara,".
4. Open with one or two friendly sentences.
5. Write the three paragraphs using linking words.
6. Close in a friendly way and sign off: "Write back soon, Ali".
7. Check the word count, spelling and tenses.
## Key ideas
### Informal language
- Contractions (I'm, can't), friendly questions, phrasal verbs.
### Useful phrases
- "Guess what!", "I can't wait to…", "By the way…", "Anyway, that's all for now."
## Worked example
**Task:** Email a friend about a school trip: where you went, what you enjoyed, what you will do next time.
**Model answer (start):** Hi Hana, Guess what! Last week our class went on a snorkelling trip to a nearby island. The water was so clear that we saw turtles and colourful fish. My favourite part was…
**Why it scores well:**
- Friendly tone and opening.
- Covers prompt one with details.
## More detail
### Layout
- Greeting: "Hi Aisha," or "Dear Ahmed,"
- Opening paragraph: friendly reply or reason for writing.
- Body paragraphs: one for each bullet point in the task.
- Closing: "Write back soon," / "Best wishes," + your first name.
### Language
- Contractions (I'm, can't), friendly questions ("Can you believe it?"), phrasal verbs (catch up, look forward to).
- Use descriptive detail and feelings to make it lively.
- Keep the tone right for the reader (a friend, a cousin, a teacher you know well).
### Useful phrases
- "It was great to hear from you."
- "Guess what happened last weekend?"
- "I can't wait to see you."
- "Let me know what you think."
### Marks
- Content: all three bullet points, developed with detail. Language: range of vocabulary, accurate grammar, linked paragraphs.
## Common mistakes
- Missing one of the three prompts.
- Using formal language ("Dear Sir").
- Going far over or under the word count.
## Easy tips
- One paragraph for each prompt.
- Add a reason or a feeling to every point.

## Overview
An article is written for a school magazine, a newsletter or a website. Your reader is usually other students. You give information and your opinions in an interesting, lively way.
- From 2024: 120–160 words, 15 marks (6 for content, 9 for language).
- Older papers: 100–150 words, 12 marks (6 + 6).
## Step-by-step method
1. Underline the topic, the reader (who reads it) and where it will be published.
2. Read the comments in the speech bubbles. They are ideas you may use, but add ideas of your own.
3. Plan 4 short paragraphs: introduction, two main points, conclusion.
4. Write a catchy title.
5. Open with a question or a surprising fact to hook the reader.
6. Give each main point a reason and an example.
7. End with your opinion or a message for the reader.
8. Check your word count, spelling and linking words.
## Key ideas
### Format
- A title is expected. It can be a question: "Should we all learn to cook?"
- No greeting (no "Dear …") and no sign-off.
- Paragraphs, each with one main idea.
### Style
- Semi-formal and friendly. You may speak directly to the reader ("Have you ever …?").
- Use a range of vocabulary and sentence types.
- Show your opinion clearly: "In my view…", "I strongly believe…".
## Useful phrases
- Opening: "Have you ever wondered…?", "Imagine a school where…"
- Adding: "What is more…", "Another reason is that…"
- Contrast: "However…", "On the other hand…"
- Ending: "So, next time you…", "All in all, I think…"
## Model opening
**Task:** An article for your school magazine about whether students should do volunteer work.
"Giving a Little, Gaining a Lot. Have you ever spent a Saturday helping someone you didn't know? Last month I joined a beach clean-up, and it changed the way I see my free time…"
## More detail
### Useful phrases
- Hook: "Have you ever wondered…?" / "Imagine waking up to…"
- Giving opinion: "In my view…" / "There is no doubt that…"
- Adding: "What is more…" / "On top of that…"
- Ending: "So, why not give it a try?" / "It's time we all…"
### Model opening
**Title: Why every student should learn to swim**
"Living on an island, we are surrounded by water every single day. Yet many young people never learn to swim properly. Here's why that needs to change."
### Checklist
- Catchy title, engaging opening, clear paragraphs, direct address to readers ("you"), strong ending.
## Common mistakes
- Writing it like a letter (Dear… / Yours…).
- Copying the speech-bubble comments word for word.
- No clear opinion at the end.
## Exam tips
- Use the bubbles as a starting point, then add at least one idea of your own.
- Keep within the word limit; extra words do not earn extra marks.

## Overview
A report is written for a head teacher, a manager or a club leader. It describes something that happened or something that exists, and ends with suggestions or recommendations.
- From 2024: 120–160 words, 15 marks (6 for content, 9 for language).
- Older papers: 100–150 words, 12 marks (6 + 6).
## Step-by-step method
1. Find the two jobs in the task, for example "say what was good" AND "suggest how it could be improved". You must do both.
2. Give the report a title.
3. Use short headings, for example: Introduction, What went well, Problems, Recommendations.
4. Introduction: say the purpose of the report.
5. Give facts and examples under each heading.
6. Finish with clear recommendations.
## Key ideas
### Format
- Title and headings help the reader. No greeting and no sign-off.
- Short, clear paragraphs.
### Style
- Formal and objective: report facts, not feelings.
- Passive forms are useful: "It was found that…", "It is recommended that…".
## Useful phrases
- "The aim of this report is to…"
- "Most students said that…", "A few people felt that…"
- "I would recommend that…", "It would be a good idea to…"
## Model opening
**Task:** A report for your head teacher about a school trip to a museum.
"Report on the Museum Trip. Introduction: The purpose of this report is to describe our Grade 10 visit to the National Museum and suggest how future trips could be improved…"
## More detail
### Useful phrases
- Purpose: "The aim of this report is to…"
- Findings: "Most students said…" / "It was found that…" / "According to the survey…"
- Recommending: "I would recommend that…" / "It would be a good idea to…"
### Model section
**Recommendations**
"I would recommend that the canteen offers more healthy options, such as fruit and salads, because many students said they would choose these if they were available."
### Checklist
- Title and short headings, formal language, facts before opinions, clear recommendations with reasons.
## Common mistakes
- Doing only one of the two jobs in the task.
- Writing it as a story or a letter.
- No recommendations at the end.
## Exam tips
- Headings make your organisation clear and quick to mark.
- Keep the tone polite and formal for the head teacher.

## Overview
A review describes something you have tried and gives your opinion of it. It ends with a recommendation. Reviews are usually for a school magazine or a website.
- From 2024: 120–160 words, 15 marks (6 for content, 9 for language).
- Older papers: 100–150 words, 12 marks (6 + 6).
## Step-by-step method
1. Say what you are reviewing and where or when you tried it.
2. Describe it briefly: what it is and what it offers.
3. Give the good points with examples.
4. Give one or two weaker points.
5. Recommend it or not, and say who would enjoy it.
## Types of review
### Place (café, restaurant, hotel, sports centre, museum)
- Location, atmosphere, service, prices, food or facilities.
- "The staff were friendly, but the queue was rather long."
### Film or television show
- Type of film, story (no spoilers), actors, music, special effects.
- "The acting was convincing, although the ending felt rushed."
### Book
- Type of book, main characters, plot (no ending), writing style.
- "The characters are so real that I could not put it down."
### Product or app/website
- What it does, how easy it is to use, value for money, problems.
- "The app is simple to use, but it needs better offline features."
### Event (festival, concert, sports day, exhibition)
- What happened, organisation, atmosphere, highlights.
- "The highlight was the student band, who had everyone dancing."
### Coursebook, magazine or other
- Content, design, how useful it is, what could be better.
## Useful phrases
- "If you are looking for…, this is the place for you."
- "The best thing about it is…", "The only disappointment was…"
- "I would definitely recommend it to…", "It is worth a visit."
## More detail
### Useful phrases
- Describing: "set in…" / "located just a short boat ride from…"
- Praising: "a must-see" / "highly recommended" / "outstanding value"
- Criticising: "a little disappointing" / "the only drawback was…"
- Recommending: "I would recommend it to anyone who…" / "Give it a miss if…"
### Model ending
"Overall, the café is a perfect spot for students on a budget. The service could be quicker, but the food more than makes up for it. Four stars from me!"
### Checklist
- Name and introduce what you are reviewing, describe the best features, mention a weakness, give a clear recommendation and who it suits.
## Common mistakes
- Only describing, with no opinion.
- Telling the whole story of a film or book.
- No recommendation at the end.
## Exam tips
- Use descriptive adjectives: delicious, crowded, gripping, user-friendly.
- Balance good and bad points, then give a clear recommendation.

## Overview
An essay is written for your teacher. It discusses a statement or question in a balanced, formal way and ends with your own view.
- From 2024: 120–160 words, 15 marks (6 for content, 9 for language).
- Older papers: 100–150 words, 12 marks (6 + 6).
## Step-by-step method
1. Read the statement. Decide: do you agree, disagree or partly agree?
2. Note two points for and two points against (the bubbles can help).
3. Plan: introduction, points for, points against, conclusion.
4. Introduction: restate the topic in your own words.
5. Body: give each point a reason or example.
6. Conclusion: give your opinion clearly and say why.
## Key ideas
### Format
- A title is optional. No greeting and no sign-off.
- Four short paragraphs work well.
### Style
- Formal: no slang and no short forms such as "don't" or "can't".
- Use impersonal phrases: "Many people believe…", "It could be argued that…".
- Balance first, then your view.
## Useful phrases
- "Some people argue that…", "Supporters of this idea claim…"
- "On the other hand…", "Critics point out that…"
- "In conclusion, I believe… because…"
## Model opening
**Task:** "Young people spend too much time on their phones." Write an essay giving your views.
"Mobile phones are now part of almost every teenager's day. While some people believe we use them too much, others argue that phones help us learn and keep in touch…"
## More detail
### Useful phrases
- Introducing a view: "Some people argue that…" / "It is often said that…"
- Contrasting: "However…" / "On the other hand…" / "Despite this…"
- Giving examples: "For instance…" / "A good example of this is…"
- Concluding: "To sum up…" / "Overall, I believe…"
### Model paragraph
"Firstly, social media helps teenagers stay connected with friends and family who live on other islands. For example, students who study in Malé can talk to their parents every day. However, spending hours online can affect sleep and schoolwork."
### Checklist
- Clear opinion, one main idea per paragraph, examples, balanced view, conclusion that answers the question.
## Common mistakes
- Giving only one side and no balance.
- Forgetting your own opinion at the end.
- Writing in a chatty, informal tone.
## Exam tips
- A clear structure earns language marks: use paragraphs and linking words.
- Your opinion in the conclusion must match what you wrote in the body.

## Overview
You hear recordings twice and answer short-answer, note-completion, matching and multiple-choice questions.
## Step-by-step method
1. Use the reading time to read every question and underline key words.
2. Predict the type of answer (number, place, name, reason).
3. On the first listening, write quick answers.
4. On the second listening, check and complete.
5. Spell answers correctly; numbers can be written as digits.
6. Answer every question.
## Key ideas
### Distractors
- Speakers often say one answer, then correct it: "on Monday… no, sorry, Tuesday".
### Signposts
- "The main reason is…", "Finally…", "However…".
## Worked example
**You hear:** "The museum used to open at nine, but now it opens at half past nine."
**Q: What time does the museum open now?**
**Answer:** 9:30
**Why it scores well:**
- It notices the change "now".
## More detail
- Read the questions before the audio starts; predict the type of answer (a number, a name, a place).
- Listen for signpost words: "but", "actually", "in fact" — the answer often follows them.
- Spell common words correctly; numbers and dates must be exact.
- On the second listening, check answers and fill gaps.
## Common mistakes
- Writing the first number heard.
- Writing too much and missing the next answer.
## Easy tips
- Write short answers; tidy them after the second listening.

## Overview
Accurate grammar and good vocabulary raise your language marks in writing. This topic covers the most common errors.
## Key ideas
### Tenses
- Present simple for habits; present continuous for now; past simple for finished actions; present perfect for experience ("I have visited…").
### Agreement
- He/She/It + verb-s: "She lives…". Everyone/each + singular verb.
### Articles and prepositions
- a/an for one of many; the for a specific one. "interested in", "good at", "depend on".
### Vocabulary
- Replace "good, nice, bad" with precise words: delicious, exciting, disappointing.
## Step-by-step method
1. After writing, read once for tenses.
2. Read again for subject–verb agreement.
3. Check articles, plurals and prepositions.
4. Replace three simple words with better ones.
## Worked example
**Correct the sentence:** "Yesterday I go to the beach and see a turtles."
**Answer:** Yesterday I went to the beach and saw a turtle.
**Why it scores well:**
- Past tense for a finished action; "a" with a singular noun.
## More detail
### Common errors to avoid
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| He don't like it | He doesn't like it |
| I am agree | I agree |
| more better | better |
| informations, advices | information, advice |
| I have went | I have gone |
| Despite of the rain | Despite the rain |
### Tenses
- Present simple (habits), present continuous (now), past simple (finished time), present perfect (experience, unfinished time), past continuous (background), future with "will" and "going to".
### Linking words
- Addition: moreover, furthermore, in addition. Contrast: however, although, whereas. Cause: because, since, as a result, therefore. Sequence: firstly, then, finally.
### Vocabulary range
- Replace overused words: good → excellent, impressive; bad → disappointing, poor; big → enormous, huge; nice → pleasant, charming.
## Common mistakes
- Mixing tenses in one story.
- "He don't" instead of "He doesn't".
## Easy tips
- Keep a list of your own common mistakes and check for them every time.
